However, only Italian bankers and merchants used double-entry bookkeeping outside of these international events until later writings spread the system across Europe.[9] In the course of the late 15th to 16th century, double-entry bookkeeping as a system was recorded and refined through the writings of Luca Pacioli, Domenico Manzoni, Barolomeo Fontana, the accountant Alvise Casanova[10], the erudite Giovanni Antonio Tagliente, and others. quation: A s s e t s = L i a b i l i t i e s + E q u i t y Every transaction recorded will keep this equation in balance. For example, a company can buy a new piece of equipment (increasing an asset), it can spend cash (reducing an asset) or take on a loan (increasing a liability). Based upon where an account sits within the accounting equation determines its normal balance - in this example, a debit to assets increases assets, whereas a credit to liabilities increases liabilities.
